summary.text: A finite totient computation produces 14,574 numbers with square totient and a 3,031-element sublist; a bit-sieve shows that every integer in the range except 158 listed cases is a sum \(n=k+\ell\) with \(k<\ell\), where both \(\phi(k)\) and \(\phi(\ell)\) are squares, so \(k<n/2\) and their product is a square. For each remaining case, a direct finite computation supplies a suitable \(k<n/2\) whose two totients have square product.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb Z:0<k<n/2\text{ and }\varphi(k)\varphi(n-k)\text{ is a square}\}.
\]
For integral \(k\), the condition \(0<k<n/2\) is equivalent to \(k\geq 1\) and \(2k<n\), or equivalently
\[
1\leq k\leq \left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus, to prove \(a(n)>0\), it is enough to exhibit one positive integer \(k\) such that \(2k<n\) and \(\varphi(k)\varphi(n-k)\) is a perfect square.

We first describe the finite calculation used below, including how all totients were evaluated.

For a positive integer \(x\), find its least prime factor \(p\) by trial division: test \(2\), and if \(x\) is odd test \(3,5,7,\ldots\), stopping either when a divisor is found or when the square of the candidate exceeds \(x\). This returns the least prime factor, since a composite integer has a prime factor no greater than its square root. Put \(y=x/p\). The standard prime-factor recurrence for Euler’s totient is
\[
\varphi(x)=
\begin{cases}
p\varphi(y),&p\mid y,\\
(p-1)\varphi(y),&p\nmid y.
\end{cases}                                                    \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, in the first case the exponent of \(p\) in \(x\) is one greater than its exponent in \(y\), so adjoining the extra factor \(p\) multiplies the totient by \(p\). In the second case \(p\) is coprime to \(y\), and multiplicativity gives \(\varphi(py)=\varphi(p)\varphi(y)=(p-1)\varphi(y)\). Together with \(\varphi(0)=0\) and \(\varphi(1)=1\), recurrence (1) computes every required totient. At each nontrivial step \(y\leq x/2\), so at most 22 recursive steps are needed for every \(x<2^{22}\). This covers all numbers in the calculation, since
\[
2{,}000{,}000<2^{22}=4{,}194{,}304.
\]
A nonnegative integer \(u\) was tested for being a square by computing \(q=\lfloor\sqrt u\rfloor\) and testing whether \(q^2=u\).

Define
\[
S=\{m:1\leq m\leq 2{,}000{,}000,\ \varphi(m)\text{ is a perfect square}\}
\]
and
\[
K=S\cap\{1,2,\ldots,199{,}999\}.
\]
An exhaustive application of (1) and the integer-square test gives
\[
|S|=14{,}574,\qquad |K|=3{,}031.                         \tag{2}
\]
Only the facts that the members found for \(S\) and \(K\) really have square totient are needed; completeness of the list of square-totient numbers is not logically necessary. The completeness is useful for stating the finite calculation succinctly.

We next formed the restricted sumset
\[
T=\{k+\ell:k\in K,\ \ell\in S,\ k<\ell\}.              \tag{3}
\]
The restriction \(k<\ell\) is crucial: if \(n=k+\ell\), it gives \(2k<n\), so that \(k\) is an admissible summand in the definition of \(a(n)\).

Here is an exact description of the finite sumset calculation. Encode \(S\) by the nonnegative integer
\[
B=\sum_{s\in S}2^s.
\]
Thus the binary digit of \(B\) in position \(j\) is 1 exactly when \(j\in S\). For each \(k\in K\), form
\[
C_k=2^{2k+1}\left\lfloor\frac{B}{2^{k+1}}\right\rfloor,
\]
and take the bitwise union \(C=\bigvee_{k\in K}C_k\). The binary digit of \(C_k\) in position \(n\) is 1 precisely when
\[
n\geq 2k+1\quad\text{and}\quad n-k\in S.
\]
The first inequality says \(n-k\geq k+1\), i.e. \(k<n-k\). Consequently the 1-bits of \(C\) are exactly the members of the restricted sumset \(T\).

The resulting finite bit-sieve shows that among the integers from 9 through \(2{,}000{,}000\), the complement of \(T\) consists of exactly the following 158 integers:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E=\{&16,21,23,24,26,28,30,31,32,43,55,63,83,96,98,99,101,104,107,112,121,132,147,152,155,167,169,179,181,228,\\
&235,243,247,263,292,315,334,337,339,343,346,350,360,373,384,408,415,419,436,460,467,503,543,595,721,722,735,749,775,782,\\
&792,811,823,841,846,851,858,860,867,891,911,918,923,935,954,966,1007,1039,1055,1122,1149,1150,1167,1215,1238,1271,1278,\\
&1323,1327,1347,1412,1507,1526,1559,1595,1642,1671,1676,1695,1742,1744,1807,1817,1823,1875,1917,1953,1966,1991,2054,2075,\\
&2102,2125,2138,2246,2293,2300,2355,2367,2435,2663,2973,2979,3030,3051,3283,3343,3408,3428,3558,3686,3741,3770,3875,3991,\\
&3992,3993,4183,4600,5447,5777,5951,6131,6215,7064,7544,9223,9593,10423,10603,11143,13423,13631,13655,16462,18451,70639,1617439\}.
                                                               \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalently, the calculation in (4) may be checked as one binary identity. Let \(D=\sum_{e\in E}2^e\). Then
\[
\left(\left\lfloor\frac{C\mathbin{\vee}D}{2^9}\right\rfloor\right)
 \bmod 2^{1{,}999{,}992}=2^{1{,}999{,}992}-1.              \tag{5}
\]
The right side has its first \(1{,}999{,}992\) binary digits all equal to 1. Since
\(9+(1{,}999{,}992)-1=2{,}000{,}000\), identity (5) says exactly that every integer in the desired interval lies either in \(T\) or in \(E\). This explains both the operation performed by the finite calculation and how its output (4) establishes complete coverage of the interval.

For every pair in (6), direct evaluation by recurrence (1), followed by the integer-square test, gives
\[
0<k,\qquad 2k<n,\qquad
\left\lfloor\sqrt{\varphi(k)\varphi(n-k)}\right\rfloor^2
   =\varphi(k)\varphi(n-k).                                  \tag{7}
\]
Thus every table entry supplies an admissible witness. This is a finite calculation of 158 pairs; it uses the same least-prime-factor recurrence (1), and (7) records all three predicates checked for each pair. Notice that all arguments of \(\varphi\) are below \(2^{22}\), so the preceding justification of the recurrence covers every evaluation in the table.

We now finish the proof. Let \(n\) satisfy
\[
9\leq n\leq 2{,}000{,}000.
\]
By the exhaustive coverage (4), there are two cases.

First suppose \(n\notin E\). Then \(n\in T\), so by (3) there are \(k\in K\) and \(\ell\in S\) such that
\[
n=k+\ell\quad\text{and}\quad k<\ell.
\]
Because \(k,\ell\in S\), there are nonnegative integers \(r,s\) with
\[
\varphi(k)=r^2,\qquad \varphi(\ell)=s^2.
\]
Also \(k>0\), and \(k<\ell\) gives
\[
2k<k+\ell=n.
\]
Since \(n-k=\ell\),
\[
\varphi(k)\varphi(n-k)=\varphi(k)\varphi(\ell)
=r^2s^2=(rs)^2.
\]
Hence this \(k\) is counted by \(a(n)\), and therefore \(a(n)>0\).

Second suppose \(n\in E\). Choose the corresponding \(k\) from table (6). Property (7) states exactly that \(k>0\), \(2k<n\), and \(\varphi(k)\varphi(n-k)\) is a perfect square. Thus this \(k\) too is counted by \(a(n)\), so again \(a(n)>0\).

Both cases prove that for every integer \(n\) with \(9\leq n\leq2\cdot10^6\), one has \(a(n)>0\), as required.
